posts.name: Mulandi Cecilia
posts.cooked:
1. Project overview and positioning / 项目概述与定位

zk-Lock is a reusable CKB lock script that conditions cell spending on a valid Groth16 proof. Any developer can write a Circom circuit, commit to its verifying key, and lock CKB cells behind it; to spend the cell, the spender submits a proof that satisfies the circuit.

The primitive is the integration layer that turns the existing on-chain Groth16 verifier into something developers can build with. The Spark-funded scope is the minimal primitive (lock script, CLI, deployed testnet artifact, and tutorial) sufficient for a developer to lock a cell behind their own circuit and unlock it end-to-end. Consumer-facing applications (web app, treasure hunt launch event) are out of scope for this grant.

2. Team profile / 团队简介

  • Name: Cecilia Mulandi
  • GitHub: CECILIA-MULANDI
  • Role: Solo developer; current participant in the CKB Builders Program (completed 12 weeks)
  • Contact: mulandicecilia4@gmail.com, Telegram @ceciliamulandi
  • Relevant prior work:
    • groth16-ckb: Groth16/BN254 verifier ported to CKB-VM, authored solo. Confirmed on Pudge testnet 2026-05-15. ~102M cycles per verification. Experimental and not yet audited. Currently in Phase 4 hardening (coverage-guided fuzzing, soundness proptests, threat model, audit prep); mainnet use is audit-gated. Public writeup on Nervos Talk: groth16-ckb: an on-chain Groth16 verifier for CKB-VM.
    • Research notes on what zero-knowledge proofs enable on CKB, published on Nervos Talk with peer review from the CKB Builders community.

3. Project background and problem statement / 项目背景与问题陈述

CKB has a working on-chain Groth16 verifier (load-bearing prior work, already shipped). What is missing is the integration layer that lets developers actually use it: there is no standard way to lock a cell behind a circuit, no convention for binding cells to specific public inputs, no tooling for a developer to go from “I have a Circom circuit” to “I have CKB locked behind it.”

The result is that zk on CKB is currently reachable only by developers who can wire together the verifier crate, lock-script scaffolding, witness encoding, and tx construction themselves. Each new use case repeats this work. The primitive does not exist as ecosystem infrastructure.

4. Solution approach / 解决方案

A single-purpose CKB lock script with one spend path: the cell unlocks iff a valid Groth16 proof matches the committed verifying key and public inputs.

Four design choices, settled during pre-proposal research:

  • vkey storage: 32-byte vk_hash in lock.args; the full verifying key lives in a shared cell_dep referenced by data_hash. Mirrors the secp256k1 system-script pattern (small commitment in args, shared data cell), so many cells can reuse one vkey cell instead of each carrying full vkey bytes.
  • Public-input binding: lock.args also carries a 32-byte public_inputs_commitment. The cell is bound to specific public inputs, not just to the circuit, which is what makes zk-Lock a primitive rather than a generic verifier wrapper.
  • Minimal lock, compose for the rest: no refund branch, no creator pubkey, no deadline. Applications that need refund or settlement (treasure hunt, auctions, escrow) layer them on via a wrapping lock or a type script. Keeps the audit surface tight and the primitive usable for sealed-bid auctions, private claims, conditional escrow, and anonymous airdrops without favouring any one of them.
  • Claimer-binding convention: circuit authors include the claimer’s lock-script hash as a public input, so a proof copied from a pending transaction cannot be redirected to another address. Enforced implicitly via public_inputs_commitment; templated in the docs and CLI.

5. Technical architecture / 技术架构

Locked cell
  lock.code_hash:  <zk-Lock script hash>
  lock.args:       vk_hash (32B) || public_inputs_commitment (32B)   = 64 bytes

Cell deps (referenced by the unlock tx)
  zk-Lock script cell                  (the code)
  vkey cell                            (data = serialized vkey; referenced by data_hash)

Witness (unlock tx)
  witness.lock:    proof || public_inputs

Script logic (built on top of the existing verifier-core crate):

  1. Read (vk_hash, public_inputs_commitment) from lock.args.
  2. Scan cell_deps; find the dep whose blake2b(data) == vk_hash. Fail if none, fail if duplicate.
  3. Read (proof, public_inputs) from witness.lock.
  4. Check hash(public_inputs) == public_inputs_commitment.
  5. Call into groth16-ckb verifier with (vk, proof, public_inputs).
  6. Return success only if all checks pass.

Off-chain pipeline:

Circom circuit  →  snarkjs proof  →  CCC SDK  →  CKB

All off-chain tooling is mature (Circom, snarkjs, CCC). All on-chain logic reuses infrastructure already shipped (groth16-ckb verifier, CKB-VM).

6. Weekly execution plan / 执行计划

Week Focus Concrete output
1 Lock script architecture; integrate groth16-ckb verifier as a lock Workspace skeleton compiles; stub lock script reads args
2 Cell-dep vkey loading; witness parsing; end-to-end test against a known-good fixture All-paths unit + integration tests pass locally
3 Deploy to CKB Pudge testnet; minimal CLI for lock/unlock; tutorial draft Testnet tx hash demonstrating a successful unlock
4 Reference Circom circuit (Poseidon hash preimage); worked end-to-end demo via CLI; documentation polish Repository, tutorial, and demo reproducible by a third party from a clean checkout

Four weeks solo. Conservative by design: explicitly avoids scope I cannot defend within Spark’s timeline (web app, wallet integration, public launch event).

7. Funding requirements / 所需资金与资金分配明细

Total request: $1,704.

Item Hours / cost Subtotal
Lock script (week 1–2): args parsing, cell-dep vkey lookup, witness decode, integration with verifier-core, unit + integration tests 70h × $12/hr $840
Testnet deployment + CLI (week 3): deploy to Pudge, lock/unlock subcommands, first successful on-chain unlock tx 42h × $12/hr $504
Reference circuit + demo + docs (week 4): Poseidon-preimage Circom circuit, snarkjs proof pipeline, tutorial markdown + short architecture reference 30h × $12/hr $360
Total 142h $1,704

Payment cadence per Spark norms: 20% upfront at project start, 80% drawn at weekly sync meetings based on demonstrated progress.

8. Deliverables and verification methods / 交付物与验证方式

Deliverable How to verify
zk-Lock script source code Public GitHub repo; cargo build --release produces riscv64imac binary; cargo test passes
Deployed lock script on Pudge testnet Cell OutPoint published in README; explorer link
Working end-to-end unlock Testnet transaction hash showing a cell unlocked by a valid Groth16 proof
Reference Circom circuit (Poseidon preimage) .circom source + snarkjs build script; reproducible vkey hash
CLI tool cargo install-able; --help documents lock and unlock subcommands
Tutorial Markdown in repo: “How to lock a cell behind your own Circom circuit”; a third party can follow it from clean checkout to a successful testnet unlock

Documentation scope: repository markdown only (README.md, tutorial, short architecture reference, CLI --help). No hosted docs site within this grant; a public-facing docs site is out of scope for this milestone.

9. Current state vs funded scope / 当前状态 vs. 资助范围

Already shipped (not funded by this grant):

  • Groth16/BN254 verifier on CKB-VM (groth16-ckb), confirmed on Pudge testnet 2026-05-15. Experimental and not yet audited.

Funded by this grant:

  • The lock-script layer that wraps the verifier as a reusable primitive.
  • CLI tooling to make the primitive usable from a terminal.
  • Reference circuit + tutorial demonstrating end-to-end use.
  • Testnet deployment of the lock script itself.

Explicitly out of scope for this grant:

  • Web app with wallet integration.
  • Public treasure hunt launch event.
  • Mainnet deployment (audit-gated; pending Phase 4 hardening of the verifier).

10. CKB ecosystem alignment / CKB 生态契合度

  • Complements existing team’s work. The SP1 verifier (XuJiandong’s team) is for complex computation; zk-Lock is for simple circuits. Both are valid, complementary use cases of zk on CKB.
  • Builds on what is already shipped. The Groth16 verifier becomes the load-bearing piece of an ecosystem primitive rather than an orphan demo.
  • Unlocks new application categories. Sealed-bid auctions, private claims, conditional escrow, and anonymous airdrops all reduce to “lock a cell behind a circuit” once the primitive exists.
  • Demonstrates the cell model and Web5 composability. Single-purpose lock + composition via wrappers and type scripts is idiomatic CKB design and aligned with the Web5 emphasis on small composable primitives layered organically rather than monolithic vertical stacks. The worked demo is intended as a reference for how to compose zk primitives in the cell model.

Risks and mitigations / 风险与缓解措施

Risk Mitigation
Verifier cycle cost is ~102M per verification (~2.9% of a block budget), limiting how many unlocks fit per block Cost is empirically measured and acceptable for the treasure-hunt-style workloads this Spark milestone targets. Optimization (precomputed pairing tables, batched verification) is deferred to a separate effort.
Mainnet deployment of the verifier is audit-gated; this grant cannot deliver mainnet artifacts Scope is explicitly testnet only (Pudge). Mainnet readiness is a separate future effort after audit and out of scope here.
groth16-ckb lives in a nested Cargo workspace; the git dependency may need a fallback to a local clone if Cargo resolution edge-cases bite Tested in week 1. Fallback (local-path dep) is documented in the README.
Tutorial reproducibility depends on Circom and snarkjs versions, which evolve Tutorial pins exact versions; CI verifies the recipe still produces the same vkey hash at each commit.

Out of scope (explicit) / 明确不在范围内

To keep evaluation crisp, this grant does not cover: web app, wallet integration, browser-side proof generation UI, mainnet deployment, public launch event with real CKB, or audit. Those are deliberately deferred to keep the Spark milestone focused on the testnet primitive.

posts.cooked:
Hi @Mulandi_Cecilia,

Thank you for your interest in the Spark Program and for submitting the zk-Lock for CKB proposal.

After review by the Spark Program committee, your proposal has been assigned a status of Pending. This is not a rejection, but an invitation to revise.

The committee recognizes the value of your project idea. The zk-Lock primitive is a meaningful piece of infrastructure for the CKB ecosystem, and we appreciate the rigorous technical background you bring from the CKB Builders Program.

Main Revision Recommendations:

  • Budget Adjustment:
    The committee has no objections to the project’s objectives and methodology, but the proposed $1704 budget does not align with the usual funding conventions for pure technical projects under the Spark Program, and no reasonable justification was provided for the excess. After careful consideration, the committee has agreed to provide funding of $900 for the project.

If your team is willing to accept the grant, please revise and resubmit according to the feedback above.
We will arrange a new round of review as soon as possible.

Best,
xingtian
On behalf of the Spark Program Committee

posts.name: Mulandi Cecilia
posts.cooked:
Hello @xingtianchunyan,

Thank you for checking in and my apologies for the delay. Today marks the end of week 2 and I have closed M1 smoothly.

M1 deliverable gate: args parsing, cell-dep vkey lookup, witness decode, integration with the Groth16 verifier from my prior groth16-ckb work which I pulled into this repo as verifier-core crate have fully been implemented and tested locally.

The lock script is located at contracts/zk-lock and it:

  • Validates the 64-byte lock args (vk_hash(32B) || pi_commitment(32B)).
  • Looks up the verifying key by scanning cell deps for a cell whose data hash matches vk_hash, mirroring the shared-vkey pattern from the proposal.
  • Parses the witness lock as proof (128) || pi_count (u32 LE) || public_inputs (pi_count × 32) and rejects malformed framing with specific error codes.
  • Recomputes blake2b_256(public_inputs) and checks it against the pi_commitment bound into the args.
  • Delegates final Groth16 verification to verifier-core.

Here is the github repo for reference: zk-Lock.

I am now moving on to M2 and should have an update posted here next week.

Thanks again.

Kind regards,
Cecilia Mulandi

  • CI deliverable has not been met, I am having some payment issues that I will be sorting before the end of today but in case it does not go to plan I will ping you here

M3 delivery gate (new since M2)

  • TypeScript SDK at sdk/ts/, covering the off-chain surface: encodeVerifyingKey, encodeProof, encodePublicInputs, hashVk, hashPi, deployVk, lock, unlock. Built on CCC.
  • Rust CLI extended with the snarkjs encoding pipeline and an offline sanity check: encode-vk, encode-proof, encode-pi, verify. The CLI now goes from snarkjs artifacts to an unlocked cell without any external tool.
  • Reproducible Circom circuit at circuits/poseidon-preimage/. build.sh pins the ptau file by blake2b-512 hash and the toolchain via package-lock.json, so any user reproduces the same vk.
  • End-to-end tutorial at docs/tutorial.md, walking from the circuit through snarkjs setup, encoding, deployment, locking, and unlocking on Pudge. The TypeScript SDK path and the Rust CLI path are documented in parallel so the reader picks their preferred stack.
  • CI workflow that pins the circuit’s vk_hash on every push and PR, as per the risks table in the proposal.

Fresh Pudge testnet run

Tutorial run against the Poseidon-preimage circuit using the current SDK:

Step Transaction
vk deploy 0x6c72cc8ad1746aa1a8bc86483cda5a579a9490241011ddaac38b400ff670a2e6
lock 0xfa4d3f1d5a67ea93aaadbd360a28e76794fcd207d05354e07c60c934f0265ef0
unlock 0x7cc857323e8d41668378ea95c6f0abdbc9f84697ce11b63ae8e18f1529264d65

A few setbacks and learnings I have had so far

Scope extension. In the proposal I originally scoped the tutorial around the TypeScript CCC path. Partway through, I realised a Rust developer coming to the repo via the CLI would still have to reach for a separate tool to encode snarkjs artifacts, which I thought would be a terrible developer experience for my fellow rust devs. So, I extended the scope a bit to build the same encoder natively in Rust and round-trip verified that both produce byte-identical output. It cost extra time, but the CLI path is now self-contained.

CI run pending. The vk_hash workflow is committed and pushed, but its first run has not completed because my GitHub account is in a stuck billing verification state (zero owed, but an authorization hold has not cleared). I have a support ticket open and will post the green run confirmation here once resolved. The workflow itself is reviewable in the repo now.

Here is the repo for reference: zk-Lock

Kind regards,
Cecilia Mulandi

Look who is taking the “no late nights” advice seriously today :).

An update on fully closing M3

I have resolved and wrapped up what was remaining when I last gave an update.

CI: the GitHub billing hold cleared. circuit-vk-hash now runs on every push and PR against both circuits, pinning:

  • poseidon-preimage (tutorial): 0x1f0424a56478f21e3890d5101ead7c3c4eaee7394dae31ed56c15e965fe82fa7
  • poseidon-preimage-bound: 0xaed87acbbd9f9e4b87bf10e910b98508b58013823a5ae86637b4d32e1e0295bf

I reached out to a few people to test and we got some feedback, credits to @truthixify who walked through the tutorial end-to-end and gave very valuable feedback.

Beyond proposal scope

The approved proposal covered the generic zk-lock only. While reviewing that script, @truthixify pointed out that it is exposed to mempool witness-copy and recipient-redirect attacks whenever a proof’s public inputs don’t bind to state that the transaction actually reads. I thought the suggestion was worth acting on, so I built a transaction-binding sibling script, zk-lock-bound. It reserves the first public input for a scalar derived from the input outpoint and the first output, then constrains that scalar on chain during verification.

Since this sits outside the original proposal, I’d love the committee to look at the PR and decide whether it belongs in the main repo: feat: adding zk-lock-bound transaction-binding script by CECILIA-MULANDI · Pull Request #4 · CECILIA-MULANDI/zk-Lock · GitHub

  • Bound contract cell: 0x9cf1e0a6ecc8eeb2705a894a828c07898e77a68a0b9d42b4ff8953bd7c569f5f:0

posts.cooked:
gm gm @xingtianchunyan and the committee,

Thank you for being direct. I think I had read the previous post and interpreted it narrowly. First, I have merged PR #4, so zk-lock-bound is now part of the main codebase. I believe it gives the project a rounder feel and also extends the use cases for teams that want to use zk-Lock. Second, I have added licenses and a contribution guideline so that others can open issues and contribute to the project independently. Third, CI now runs the build and the full test suite on every push and pull request, not just the circuit vk_hash pin I mentioned earlier, so a contributor finds out whether their change is sound without waiting on me.

The project was posted in the CKBuilders TG group and I also did DM a few builders that had interacted with the groth16 verifier to get their feedback on this project, and we received feedback. One piece came from @truthixify, which was addressed in PR #4. Another came from @ArthurZhang, who assessed M1 and tagged the project. He also went through the project after we delivered M3 and gave feedback on the flow and clarity of the tutorial, which was addressed. @OWK50GA also went through the tutorial, and we had a discussion on some design choices, specifically why witness.lock is a flat positional layout rather than Molecule.

That discussion and the reasoning behind the design choices are now documented in docs/encoding-rationale.md, including a few open questions I would rather not settle on my own. Anyone is welcome to open an issue on those, or on anything else in the repo, whether it is a bug or just a discussion.

My immediate next moves are outward rather than inward: supporting the people building on this work, and on the verifier it sits on

Kind regards,
Cecilia Mulandi
